name: Clavicular's looksmaxxing philosophy

lead: Clavicular is the online alias of Braden Peters, an American streamer who became prominent in 2025 and 2026 on Kick and TikTok. His approach, called 'hardmaxxing' by followers, is a maximal template for 'ascension': a sharper face, a leaner physique and a more commanding presence.

The chain runs through an aggressive mindset, then anabolic steroids, injectable peptides, extreme dieting and bonesmashing, aimed at changing face and body. The appearance claims come from his streams and anecdote rather than trials, and medical sources describe bonesmashing as pseudoscientific.

paras: Followers treat the approach as a package: streams and clips for the mindset, a paid course that includes guides on injectable peptides, and a mix of drug use, strict dieting and physical modification. People combine it with standard looksmaxxing steps such as fitness and skincare, and results are described over months to years.

Critics, including doctors, argue the content harms young men, and bonesmashing is described by medical sources as dangerous. Wikipedia's looksmaxxing article says he overdosed on a livestream in 2026 after a five-drug 'pentastack'. Legal matters reported include arrests, some with charges dropped, and a September 2026 Massachusetts charge that he denies and which remains an allegation.

chain: Pursuit of a sharper face and physique
angle.text: Followers of streamer Clavicular use his approach as a template for maximal 'ascension': an aggressive mindset plus drug protocols, bonesmashing talk and extreme self-improvement aimed at a more striking face and physique. The appearance claims come from his streams and anecdote rather than trials, and medical sources have criticised the approach.

lead: Clavicular is the online alias of Braden Eric Peters, an American streamer born in December 2005 and raised in Hoboken, New Jersey, who became one of the best-known looksmaxxing influencers through Kick and TikTok in 2025 and 2026.[1] The alias comes from the community's emphasis on clavicle (shoulder) width as part of a broad, imposing frame.[1] His content presents looksmaxxing as a route to looking better and succeeding socially, which he calls ascending.[1]

Peters describes looksmaxxing as taking self-improvement to its logical conclusion. In a July 2026 Fox News interview he said it combines traditional bodybuilding and fitness with a new focus on facial aesthetics, and argued that male self-improvement culture had neglected the face.[2] His stated reasoning is that appearance affects employment and everyday interactions, not only dating.[2] Followers describe the practical goals as a wider frame, a leaner face, a sharper jaw and a higher rating on community scales such as PSL.[1][3]

The practices associated with his content range from training and grooming through to hardmaxxing: anabolic steroids and testosterone, methamphetamine as an appetite suppressant, peptides, fat-dissolving injections, cosmetic surgery and bonesmashing, which Wikipedia calls pseudoscientific.[1][3] He sold a paid course, first the Clavicular System and later Clavicular's Clan, with guides on ascending that include injectable peptides.[1] Coverage in The New York Times, The Atlantic, The Guardian, Rolling Stone, Wired and other outlets has treated him as the public face of the movement in 2026, alongside reporting on bans, arrests, a suspected overdose and legal proceedings, summarised below.[1]

paras: Peters was raised in Hoboken, New Jersey; Wikipedia reports that his father is a businessman and his mother a former bodybuilder.[1] He says he became interested in looksmaxxing in high school and spent much of the COVID-19 lockdowns online, reportedly around 14 hours a day.[1] He attended Sacred Heart University in Connecticut for about three weeks before being expelled, reportedly for using peptides and steroids.[1]

He has said he began testosterone injections at 14, and that he is on the autism spectrum, though he has no professional diagnosis.[1] He has also described himself as Catholic and apolitical, while commentators have placed him within the manosphere and the so-called Very Online Right.[1] He lived in Miami by 2026.[1]

According to Know Your Meme's record, the earliest surviving Instagram post is from October 2024, captioned "Mogged", and the earliest surviving TikTok from April 2025; he began streaming on Kick on 27 May 2025 and streamed regularly from mid-November 2025.[4] A TikTok with his girlfriend on 15 November 2025 passed 7.9 million views, a subreddit named for him was created on 1 November 2025, and video essays by YouTubers followed that month and in December.[4]

His reach grew through clippers, accounts that repost short pieces of livestreams with captions, often for money.[1] A December 2025 clip in which he said Gavin Newsom looked better than JD Vance spread widely on X and helped popularise mogging as a mainstream term.[4] In February 2026 a tweet about a fraternity leader at Arizona State University produced the phrase frame mog, which Wikipedia describes as a viral term from his orbit.[1][4] The New York Times' Joseph Bernstein reported earnings above $100,000 a month on Kick by February 2026.[1]

Mainstream attention peaked in early 2026, with profiles in The Atlantic, Rolling Stone, The Guardian, GQ and The New York Times, a New York runway appearance for the designer Elena Velez in February, and a Paris show opening in June.[1] Wired had profiled him in September 2025.[1]

The central idea is ascension: that men can raise their attractiveness and, with it, their social standing and success.[1] He has argued in interviews that appearance affects every interaction, and that the face has been missing from the male self-improvement tradition, which focused on physique.[2] He also ties his nightlife streams to hypergamy, saying they show how few men succeed with women, a framing reported by Fox News.[2]

Wikipedia lists terms associated with him. Ascend means becoming more attractive and successful; hardmaxx means undergoing intense or painful physical alterations; mogging means being more attractive than someone else; frame mogging means being out-sized by someone with a bigger frame; and jestermaxxing means having fun, which he has called the opposite of politics and a foolish waste of time.[1] Wikipedia's looksmaxxing article distinguishes softmaxxing (skincare, grooming, clothing, fitness, mewing) from hardmaxxing (steroids, peptides, growth hormone, extreme dieting, surgery); his content sits at the hardmaxxing end.[3]

He has said looksmaxxing is a way out of incel culture rather than part of it, and in a 60 Minutes Australia interview in April 2026 he walked out after being asked whether he was an incel.[1] Commentators disagree: UnHerd's critique describes his teaching as incel-influenced ideas about earning women's attention by becoming a Chad, while arguing that his real audience is other men and the status competition among them.[5] Spiked, as summarised by Wikipedia, called him a parody of masculinity, while Rolling Stone wrote that his optimisation is inseparable from sexism.[1]

Wikipedia lists traditional bodybuilding and fitness training, a newer focus on facial aesthetics, anabolic steroids and testosterone, methamphetamine for appetite suppression, Adderall, Accutane, retatrutide, nebivolol, peptides and fat-dissolving injections among the methods he has discussed or shown.[1] He has publicly discussed using meth to curb appetite, and says steroid use left him infertile.[1][6] UnHerd also reports makeup techniques, face rating of strangers and advice to fans to get nose jobs.[5]

Bonesmashing, striking the facial bones to try to reshape the jaw or cheekbones, is associated with his content; Wikipedia calls it pseudoscientific, and Fox News describes medical experts warning of serious injury, while noting he was not quoted describing it in that interview.[1][2] He himself had a rhinoplasty in June 2026; The Daily Beast reported that fans criticised the result, saying he lost his unique facial character.[7]

By late 2025 he sold a subscription course for about 50 dollars a month, with guides on how to ascend and suggestions of peptides to inject, according to coverage cited by Wikipedia from The Independent and Intelligencer.[1] Rolling Stone's Charlie Sabgir paid 49 dollars for access when reporting on it, and UnHerd reports higher-priced packages of 5,000 dollars or more.[1][5]

Other ventures reported by Wikipedia include sponsorship by the online casino Duel, a stake in a Miami nightclub that opened in April 2026 and that he later said he had sold, and a campus tour in August 2026 where two events were cancelled over safety concerns or planned protests.[1] A lawsuit relating to the nightclub was reported.[1]

YouTube terminated his original channel in November 2025 for facilitating access to sites that violate its policies on illegal or regulated goods and services.[8] On 23 April 2026 it terminated two further channels, @LiveWithClav and @ClavLooksmax, citing severe or repeated violations of its community guidelines and its rule against creating new channels after a termination; Peters said they were removed without warning.[8] A December 2025 livestream incident led to a Kick ban; he said he had acted in self-defence.[1]

On 14 April 2026 his Kick stream was cut off after fellow influencer Androgenic offered him a pill during an outing in Miami; Androgenic wrote that Peters became fairly unresponsive within seconds, and the group took him to hospital.[6] The Hollywood Reporter, People and CBS News reported a suspected overdose; Global News noted that which substances he took was not publicly confirmed.[6] Wikipedia's looksmaxxing article attributes the episode to a combination known as the pentastack, which Androgenic had previously described and later defended.[3]

Peters said he was released the next day, called the experience brutal and said that substances were a way of coping with trying to feel neurotypical in public.[6] In July 2026 he said the suspected overdose had been misreported, according to Us Weekly as cited by Wikipedia.[1]

Wikipedia cites profiles in The New York Times, The Atlantic, The Guardian, Rolling Stone, Intelligencer, Spiked, GQ, CNN, Le Monde and Wired.[1] The Atlantic called him the newest star of the looksmaxxing movement, Intelligencer called him something of an edgelord folk hero, and Spiked argued he is better understood as a parody of masculinity than a right-wing thought leader.[1] UnHerd presented him as a salesman who nonetheless seems to believe in his methods, and observed that boys are now openly performing body-image rituals long associated with teenage girls.[5] A March 2026 Guardian column compared his methods to body dysmorphia.[1]
Academic work has also appeared: Wikipedia lists a 2026 paper in the Journal of Stomatology, Oral and Maxillofacial Surgery and one in the Journal of Humanistic Psychology among its references.[1]

Wikipedia reports that Peters has used racial slurs on stream and in TikToks, which he has treated as humour, and that he has been accused of promoting misogyny and incel-linked ideas, which he denies.[1] In January 2026 he was among a group, including Nick Fuentes, that sang along to a song containing a Nazi salute in a Miami Beach club; he called it just a song, and the city's mayor condemned the incident.[1] A November 2025 video showed him injecting his then-17-year-old girlfriend with fat-dissolving peptides, and critics argue his content harms young men.[1][5]

On 24 December 2025 a livestream appeared to show him driving a vehicle into a man in Miami-Dade County; he said it was self-defence, and Kick banned him.[1][4] Events in 2026 reported by Wikipedia include a 7 February Arizona arrest for drug possession and a fake-ID charge, dropped on 11 February; a late-March Florida battery arrest; a plea deal on an alligator-shooting charge with probation and community service; and a civil suit filed in April, in which the sexual-assault claims were later reportedly dropped.[1]

On 8 September 2026 he was charged in Massachusetts in connection with an alleged May 2025 incident involving a 17-year-old. He pleaded not guilty in October and denies the charges, which remain allegations.[1]

Wikipedia's looksmaxxing article reports that commentators criticise the movement as judgmental and link it to body dysmorphia, that its advice relies heavily on anecdote rather than mainstream medicine, and that doctors have criticised bonesmashing and mewing as misinformation, citing fracture and other injury risks.[3] The same article notes that some men report benefits such as social affirmation or dating success after improving their appearance.[3]
No studies found.

lore.intro: Clavicular's content and vocabulary are widely discussed in looksmaxxing spaces, on r/Clavicular and in mainstream media; the entries below describe how his philosophy is characterised, not an endorsement.[1][3][4]
